stances.claim: Moderate at best and spotty at worst is the recent government effort to decongest traffic on the 28.3-km Edsa -- but for the first week, the effort was good enough despite the Tuesday-night carmageddon and its near-repetition Thursday; authorities must do better in coming weeks

From Monday Sept 7, smartly-uniformed PNP-HPG motorcycle units under direct Palace supervision instilled discipline, arrested recalcitrant drivers/pedestrians, shooed away colorums and provincial buses, cleared peddlers and illegally-parked vehicles, directed buses to stay inside yellow lanes, and allowed no more than 30 seconds to load and unload passengers

'Voila!' Several choke points were decongested and traffic flowed, even if intermittently -- southbound from Balintawak/North/QC Ave/Cubao eased considerably; but northbound from Makati to Guadalupe/Shaw/Ortigas/Cubao was still crawling

These immediate solutions including the PNP-HPG deployment were suggested by MAP's Traffic-Transportation-Infrastructure Committee chaired by Eddie Yap -- two months earlier MAP submitted a 'holistic approach' arguing traffic problems are 'behavioral and structural' to be addressed through the three Es: traffic engineering, education of all stakeholders, and enforcement of traffic rules

MAP strongly suggested appointing a 'traffic czar' -- 'elementary it is in the science of management that someone must always be responsible for the success or failure of any undertaking'; despite the lack of an official appointment, Cabinet Secretary Rene Almendras is effectively performing the role per Yap: 'Rene talks like a czar, acts like a czar and is a czar except in name'

It is now time to implement other MAP recommendations: include all intersecting avenues (Buendia, Shaw, Ortigas, D. Tuazon) and radial roads (C5, Katipunan, Roxas); organize a bus dispatch system; channelize Edsa with more bus-lane delineators; flood-proof low street levels using WW2-era prefab steel perforated matting on steel supports; install HOV lane for 3+ passenger vehicles; encourage carpools and bus shuttles

Longer-term MAP proposals include new Pasig River bridges, resolving MRT/LRT issues, constructing subway systems, educating drivers and pedestrians on traffic rules and road courtesy, and undertaking more effective flood control

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a first-week review of the government's Edsa traffic-decongestion effort: 'moderate at best and spotty at worst,' but good enough for week one -- despite the nightmarish 'carmageddon' Tuesday night due to a massive downpour, and its scary near-repetition Thursday saved this time by the presence of drenched cops and traffic enforcers. The authorities must do better in coming weeks. From Monday, Sept 7, the smartly-uniformed, motorcycle-riding and sufficiently-armed cops fielded by the PNP-HPG, under direct Palace supervision, instilled discipline among drivers and pedestrians, arrested the recalcitrant, and shooed away colorums and provincial buses. The PNP-HPG also cleared the thoroughfare of peddlers and illegally-parked vehicles, ordered walkers to use marked pedestrian lanes, directed buses to stay inside the yellow lanes, and allowed them no more than 30 seconds to load and unload passengers. And 'voila!' -- several choke points were decongested and traffic flowed, even if intermittently. Quite pleased were motorists from the northern end of Edsa going south to Makati: with the clearing of hawkers and towing of illegally-parked vehicles at Balintawak, North Ave, Quezon Ave, and Cubao, coupled with strict enforcement, southbound traffic considerably eased. However, going northward -- especially from Makati to Guadalupe, Shaw Boulevard, Ortigas Avenue, and Cubao intersections -- traffic was still quite heavy and vehicles were still crawling. The downpours on Tuesday and Thursday simply overwhelmed the antique drainage system. These immediate solutions, including the PNP-HPG deployment, were suggested by the Traffic, Transportation and Infrastructure Committee of the MAP, chaired by the energetic Eddie Yap. Two months ago MAP submitted to P-Noy a 'holistic approach' arguing 'the traffic problems besetting our metropolis are behavioral and structural,' to be addressed through 'the three most basic elements, the three Es, of effective traffic management: traffic engineering, education of all stakeholders, and enforcement of traffic rules.' After reading the study, CJ waited to find out what Malacañang would do -- and sure enough, starting last Monday, many of the MAP proposals were implemented and followed through the whole week. Significantly, MAP strongly suggested the appointment of a 'traffic czar' to take full charge and assume responsibility for success or failure: 'Elementary it is in the science of management that someone must always be responsible for the success or failure of any undertaking.' Despite the lack of an official appointment, Cabinet Secretary Rene Almendras is effectively performing the role per Yap: 'Rene talks like a czar, acts like a czar and is a czar except in name' -- though one broadsheet (not the Inquirer) has bannered Almendras' supposedly formal appointment as traffic supremo. With or without a czar, it is now time to implement other MAP recommendations: include all intersecting avenues (Buendia, Shaw, Ortigas, D. Tuazon) and radial roads (C5, Katipunan, Roxas); organize a bus dispatch system; 'channelize' Edsa with more bus-lane delineators; flood-proof low street levels using prefabricated quick-to-assemble steel perforated matting on steel supports similar to those used by the US during WW2 as an emergency measure while awaiting permanent concrete upgrading; install a high-vehicle-occupancy lane for vehicles with at least three passengers; encourage carpools and bus shuttles. Longer-term MAP proposals include new Pasig River bridges, resolving MRT/LRT issues, high-capacity subway systems, educating drivers and pedestrians on traffic rules and road courtesy, and effective flood control. In the past, the government had the wrong focus -- instead of optimizing road usage, it tried to curtail demand by reducing work days, suspending classes, and instituting truck bans, exacting a heavy toll on the economy and the patience of the riding public. As ECOP president Eduardo Lacson lamented, 'The proposal for a four-day workweek is a solution begging for a problem ... It poses risks of accident, low performance, off-spec products due to worker fatigue born of long work hours.' Indeed, we as a people should think more horizontally and avoid what former PM Cesar Virata calls 'short-termism' -- the 'excessive focus on short-term goals at the expense of long-term objectives.'
